This paper introduces a novel approach to survival analysis that utilizes presmoothing to generate weighted contributions for survival data. By applying this method to a survival model, we establish the asymptotic normality of the resulting estimators. We demonstrate that this presmoothing technique yields superior performance compared to maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) in terms of both bias and asymptotic variance. Furthermore, we extend this framework to accommodate censored data and confirm that the resulting estimator remains asymptotically Gaussian. These findings are illustrated through a numerical example, and the paper concludes by discussing the broader implications of the proposed method.

This study introduces the concept of nonlocal metric dimension, denoted as $ \text{ndim}(G) $, for a connected graph $ G $, and investigates its fundamental properties. We derive a formula to calculate this dimension and provide a characterization for graphs where $ \text{ndim}(G) $ equals 1 or $ n(G)-2 $. Additionally, we present several algorithms for determining nonlocal metric sets and analyze the graph classes for which $ \text{ndim}(G) $ equals $ n(G)-2 $.

This study examines the vulnerability of neural network architectures to side-channel attacks utilizing power trace data. We introduce a novel attack methodology that leverages power measurements to recover the input data of a target network. The core of this approach involves a specialized network, termed a "side-channel decoder," which is trained to reconstruct the input data of a target network from a single power measurement. The training process utilizes a synthetic data generator that produces realistic power trace data based on the input data of a target network. We demonstrate the efficacy of this attack by successfully recovering MNIST images from a target network with 99.8% accuracy using merely 10 power measurements per image.

This paper introduces a new approach to optimize the shortening of polarization kernels, which are fundamental to polarized signal processing. By utilizing bounds derived from partial distances, the study establishes a fresh distance metric that enables the derivation of simplified kernels with reduced weight. This methodology is applied to correct the distance definitions found in prior literature and to generate upper and lower bounds for a newly proposed distance. Furthermore, numerical results demonstrate that the suggested metric effectively accelerates the shortening procedure, producing significantly fewer error correction codewords compared to established methods.

This study introduces a new self-supervised learning framework designed to denoise seismic data. The approach utilizes initial supervised training on a synthetic dataset to generate a network capable of predicting clean traces from noisy inputs. This preliminary training accelerates the self-supervised phase by enabling the model to learn noise removal patterns immediately, thereby reducing the reliance on large volumes of real seismic data. The efficacy of this method is validated using a real-world dataset of noisy seismic recordings. The findings demonstrate that the synthetic data not only facilitates the initial supervised training but also sustains high performance levels during the subsequent self-supervised training.

This study examines the impact of real photon emission on the charge asymmetry of the $W$-boson production process in lepton-proton collisions. We demonstrate that the inclusion of these emissions is essential for accurately calculating the charge asymmetry within the framework of collinear factorization.

We investigate the electronic structure of Mott insulators within the Hubbard model, specifically focusing on the interplay between the spin-polaronic ladder spectrum and the spin gap. Our findings demonstrate that the spin-polaronic ladder spectrum significantly reshapes the electronic structure of Mott insulators, a phenomenon that is further modulated by the spin gap magnitude.

This paper introduces a novel estimator for continuous treatment effects that extends the recent double-robust framework of Cui et al. (2020). While retaining their property that consistent performance relies on satisfying only either the positivity or robustness assumption, this new approach additionally offers a direct extension to scenarios involving multiple treatments. We further demonstrate that this estimator achieves double robustness within the context of multiple treatments, provided the analysis is confined to causal effects that are identifiable. We evaluate the estimator's performance through simulations and apply it to an empirical case study examining the relationship between antidepressant medication usage and patient recovery outcomes.

The recent popularity of starshades has led to a surge in research, resulting in a large and growing body of literature that remains difficult to navigate. This paper introduces a curated bibliography of starshades, designed to help newcomers to the field and to foster collaboration among established researchers. By organizing recent developments, the bibliography facilitates easier discovery of overlapping interests, such as co-located research opportunities, for professionals in this domain. The article also outlines the criteria used for selecting entries and provides a link to the complete bibliography, which is also available on GitHub.

Detecting suicidal content online is critical for safeguarding mental health, yet existing resources are limited by small datasets, outdated data, or restricted demographics. To address this, we introduce the **Robin** dataset, a collection of 1.1 million tweets from 2018 that have been manually annotated for suicidal intent. This dataset is designed to support research on identifying suicidal text within English social media, specifically among young adults. We also provide a detailed analysis of how the Robin dataset enhances prior resources, along with baseline models and a comparison of their performance. These resources are intended to facilitate the development of effective suicide prevention strategies.

We present a supersymmetric framework for the Schwarzian derivative, derived from super-constraints on a supersymmetric Schwarzian object. This approach yields a supersymmetric analogue of the super-Schwarzian action, which subsequently reduces to the well-known bosonic Schwarzian action upon localization to the bosonic slice.

This paper addresses the issue of determining rational dynamical systems and difference equations from their orbits, presenting several novel findings with significant implications in coding theory, cryptography, and the area of inverse problems within dynamical systems theory.

This study examines the coupling of Einstein's General Relativity with nonlinear electrodynamics within the presence of an electrically charged AdS black hole. We derive the black hole's thermodynamic properties and analyze the corresponding phase transitions. Furthermore, we establish the holographic correspondence for this setup, utilizing the metric of the extended thermodynamic phase space to construct a holographic model of the system.

This study examines the geometric phase in a spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain subjected to a transverse magnetic field, utilizing exact diagonalization. We demonstrate that magnetic susceptibility exhibits a direct proportionality to the geometric phase within this system. By analyzing the quantum phase transition occurring at the critical field, we observe a singularity in the geometric phase. Furthermore, we establish a quantitative correlation between the magnitude of this phase and the correlation length, confirming a direct proportionality.

This study examines the relaxation of ferromagnets from elevated temperatures within the mean-field framework, specifically focusing on the influence of critical fluctuations. We demonstrate that these fluctuations can be incorporated into the magnetization's time-dependent evolution equation via a time-varying susceptibility. The resulting model is validated against experimental data from $\text{FeCl}_2$ and $\text{FeCl}_2\cdot4\text{H}_2\text{O}$, as well as simulations of the Ising model, confirming its applicability. Furthermore, the analysis yields a time-dependent activation energy, which is shown to be consistent with the activation energies derived from the isothermal magnetization curves.

This study examines the localization transition for bound states in quasicrystals, focusing on the interplay between the quasiperiodic potential and the on-site energy. We derive an analytical expression for the eigenenergies of bound states and demonstrate that they exhibit a power-law dependence on the ratio of the potential strength to the on-site energy. Furthermore, we establish a precise criterion for the transition to localization, showing that the associated eigenstates become delocalized when this ratio surpasses a specific threshold.

Current multilingual task-oriented dialogue systems primarily depend on data from English-language datasets, which are then adapted for other languages via translation. This approach often results in suboptimal performance, particularly for complex tasks. To address this, we introduce a new method for constructing multilingual task-oriented dialogue datasets by leveraging the structural similarities between different language versions of the same task. We have developed a specific framework to automate the creation of these datasets, which involves translating natural language instructions and user utterances while preserving the task schema. We have applied this framework to build a multilingual dataset for the ATIS task covering 11 languages. Our evaluation demonstrates that training a domain adaptation model using our newly constructed dataset significantly enhances the performance of a baseline system.

We introduce a streamlined approach for analyzing RNA-seq time series data, capable of identifying differential expression and alternative splicing. By employing a two-part linear model, we assess the significance of a time coefficient for the mean and for the ratio of the two components of that mean. This approach is computationally efficient, allowing for the simultaneous analysis of multiple conditions and the estimation of a variance-covariance matrix for the resulting time series coefficients. We demonstrate the method's utility through a case study on the temporal splicing patterns of the *MARCHF1* gene, alongside a thorough evaluation of its statistical properties using simulated datasets.

The increasing adoption of data-driven technologies has heightened the necessity for strict privacy protection. To address this, the GDPR introduced a mandatory requirement for data controllers to implement "appropriate technical measures" to secure personal data. Nevertheless, the legal language describing these measures remains vague, leaving the specific duties of both engineering and legal teams unclear. This ambiguity hinders effective collaboration between the two groups when implementing technical safeguards. This paper addresses that issue by proposing a structured, step-by-step methodology for translating privacy law into actionable technical measures. Our approach is designed to foster better communication and cooperation between legal and engineering teams throughout the entire process of implementing technical measures to ensure compliance with GDPR.

The Color Glass Condensate formalism offers a framework to investigate the azimuthal cumulant for sets of particles, derived from a framework where the cumulant is expressed as a Fourier coefficient. We derive the fourth-order cumulant for four particles, demonstrating that it is proportional to the four-particle correlation function. Furthermore, we derive the corresponding analytical results for the fourth-order cumulant in the specific kinematic limit where all particles share the same transverse momentum.

This study examines the production of light nuclei within a hydrodynamic framework, specifically analyzing coalescence mechanisms in heavy-ion collisions at the LHC. We investigate the impact of coalescence sources on deuteron and helium-3/4 transverse momentum spectra and rapidity distributions, alongside their elliptic flow ($v_2$) and nuclear modification factors ($R_{\mathrm{AA}}$). Our results indicate that coalescence sources significantly enhance the yields of light nuclei at low transverse momentum, thereby increasing the effective coalescence temperature. Furthermore, we observe that the $v_2$ for these nuclei is primarily dictated by the $v_2$ of their constituent nucleons, whereas the $R_{\mathrm{AA}}$ is mainly governed by the $R_{\mathrm{AA}}$ of free nucleons.

The discovery of numerous rocky exoplanets has revealed a wide variety of atmospheric compositions, including those that are hydrogen-dominated, water-rich, or nitrogen-rich. This study examines how the atmospheric composition of rocky planets is shaped by their formation and evolution, specifically focusing on the influence of the initial volatile inventory and the subsequent loss of primordial atmospheres. We demonstrate that the atmospheric composition of a rocky planet is primarily determined by its volatile inventory and the temperature at which its atmosphere is lost. Our findings indicate that rocky planets in the habitable zone of M-dwarf stars exhibit a wide range of atmospheric compositions, including hydrogen-dominated, water-rich, and nitrogen-rich environments. Furthermore, we find that the atmospheric composition of a rocky planet is largely independent of its mass and radius. These results underscore the importance of considering the volatile inventory and the temperature at which atmospheric loss occurs when predicting the atmospheric composition of rocky planets.

This paper investigates the dispersability of circulant graphs $C_{n}(j)$, defined by a prime order $n$ and a jump length $j$ satisfying $2 \leq j \leq \lfloor n/2\rfloor$. We demonstrate that when $j$ is restricted to no more than 3, these properties are governed by the specific arithmetic characteristics of $n$. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound for dispersability applicable to all circulant graphs.

This paper investigates the convergence characteristics of the Nested Neumann algorithm, which is designed to solve the challenge of computing the inverse of the determinant of a matrix. The study demonstrates that the algorithm's inception depth critically influences its convergence rate. Leveraging this finding, we introduce a method to determine an appropriate depth for each iteration, which significantly enhances computational efficiency. Furthermore, we analyze the algorithm's performance when applied to calculating the permanent of a matrix, and we evaluate its efficacy across both real-world and synthetic datasets.

This study examines the boost effects on curvature perturbuations within a single-field inflationary model featuring a "cosmic friction" term in the perturbation equation, which is proportional to the perturbation's time derivative. We demonstrate that, contrary to standard expectations, the standard boost effects are suppressed by the friction term. Consequently, the resulting perturbations deviate from the standard Lorentz-invariant plane wave form, exhibiting instead a complex structure.

This study examines how airlines' pricing strategies are influenced by their ability to offer price levels that are too high for some consumer segments to afford. Airlines can either set a single uniform price or implement a two-tiered system with a high price and a lower, rationed price. The research demonstrates that a simple two-tiered model effectively captures the nuances of restricted fare offerings, including demand generation, displacement, and scenarios where neither strategy outperforms the other. Crucially, the model accounts for consumer segmentation based on price sensitivity and the inherent costs of managing two different fare structures. The findings reveal that airlines may choose to offer no discount at all, or alternatively, restrict discount availability for certain segments. The model also analyzes how varying consumer heterogeneity and cost structures influence these pricing decisions.

The survival package in casebase extends the capabilities of the traditional survival model to incorporate complex covariates. This new tool offers a more straightforward approach to survival data analysis compared to conventional methods. By providing a suite of functions for survival analysis, it enables the construction of survival models that account for both time-to-event outcomes and covariates with an ordinal scale.

We introduce a novel semi-numerical technique for computing the three-loop massless scalar box integral, which significantly streamlines the numerical evaluation of the scalar sector in multi-loop processes involving massive particles. This method achieves a substantial reduction in numerical errors, lowering the relative uncertainty by a factor of approximately 100 compared to prior semi-analytical results. By employing a new strategy that derives the integral's second derivative with respect to mass via numerical integration, we subsequently calculate the integral itself through numerical integration of the resulting equation. This approach yields results with precision levels of $10^{-7}$ to $10^{-8}$, contingent on the specific kinematic configuration. Furthermore, we detail the implementation of the method within the \texttt{Fan} program package and provide a comprehensive comparison of its performance against other existing semi-analytical and numerical tools.

Distributed POSIX file systems, such as Lustre, have long been constrained by scalability issues stemming from their reliance on centralized components like name servers and metadata servers. In contrast, object storage systems, exemplified by Ceph, achieve scalability by decoupling metadata from data storage. This paper introduces a novel POSIX file system that separates metadata and storage into two distinct layers, enabling independent scaling for each. The system utilizes a distributed metadata service modeled after the key-value store in Cassandra, while data resides in a shared storage pool. This architecture allows for flexible data distribution, including support for both object storage and block devices.

This study examines the pricing mechanisms for charging electric vehicles (EVs) within parking facilities, specifically addressing scenarios where charging infrastructure is scarce. We introduce a new framework that accounts for EVs arriving sequentially and fluctuating electricity prices, alongside the dynamic availability of charging units. The primary goal is to maximize the aggregator's revenue by balancing the trade-off between the revenue from selling electricity and the income generated from parking fees. We demonstrate that the optimal charging allocation policy is time-dependent, with the number of active chargers varying based on the current electricity rate. Furthermore, we propose a new online learning algorithm designed to estimate the underlying time-varying electricity prices and simultaneously determine the most profitable parking and charging fees. Simulation results indicate that this learning method significantly outperforms existing benchmarks.

This study introduces a new methodology to generate extended LCD Hermitic codes by utilizing the self-orthogonal properties of existing codes. Furthermore, we present an approach to constructing Hermitian LCD codes by combining two arbitrary codes. We illustrate the efficacy of these techniques with several newly discovered linear codes characterized by diverse parameters.

We present the first comprehensive analysis of black-hole scattering within Einstein's gravity coupled to scalar fields, specifically examining the case of a single scalar. Our investigation focuses on the first non-trivial contribution to the black-hole S-matrix, which corresponds to the $O(G^2)$ term in the black-hole potential. This calculation relies on a set of integrals that are evaluated up to the required order, with the resulting $O(G^2)$ black-hole potential derived for both the Einstein-Scalar (ES) and Einstein-axion scalar (EAS) theories. Furthermore, we derive the first subleading corrections to the black-hole metric, specifically the $O(G^3)$ terms, for both ES and EAS models. Finally, we calculate the first non-trivial deflection angle for a scalar particle moving in the background of a black-hole, extending to the $O(G^2)$ order for both theoretical frameworks.

Achieving clean electricity goals within affordable limits depends heavily on the land-use implications of proposed solar and wind projects. This study evaluates the risk of land conflicts by integrating a land-use model with a power system model, revealing that the feasibility of meeting these goals is highly sensitive to the specific land-use risk assigned to these sites. We demonstrate that the necessity for backup capacity in low-density regions significantly influences land-based risk, thereby affecting the overall cost of attaining clean electricity. Additionally, we find that the necessity for such backup can be mitigated by strategically selecting new solar and wind locations, which in turn lowers land-based risk and the total expense of clean energy targets.

In cluster-randomized trials (CRTs) conducted in community settings, vaccination is administered to individuals within specific clusters, generating both direct effects on vaccinees and indirect (herd) effects on non-vaccinated persons. Distinguishing between these two components is vital for forecasting the true population-level impact of vaccination. While CRTs are frequently employed to measure these effects, estimating the direct component remains a significant challenge. Standard methods for isolating direct effects in CRTs depend on combining data from multiple clusters across different time periods, a strategy that is often unfeasible due to insufficient sample sizes. This paper introduces a new approach to estimate direct effects by leveraging the contrast between CRTs and observational studies. This technique is particularly useful when observational data are abundant and can be integrated with CRT information. We propose a novel framework that utilizes the difference between CRTs and observational studies to adjust for unmeasured confounding, thereby enabling the estimation of direct effects. To implement this framework, we introduce a new estimator that combines data from CRTs and observational studies, utilizing inverse probability weighting to adjust for selection bias. We demonstrate that this estimator is asymptotically unbiased and consistent, and we evaluate its performance through simulations. Finally, we apply this method to estimate the direct effects of influenza vaccination using data from the CDC's Vaccine Safety Datalink (VSD) study, which includes both CRTs and observational datasets.

This study derives a closed-form expression for the multiplicative degree-Kirchhoff index applicable to any network, expressed through its Laplacian eigenvalues and the node degrees of an entire graph. Furthermore, we present an algorithm for calculating this multiplicative index and derive approximation formulas for both unweighted and weighted graphs. Additionally, the research offers a closed-form calculation for the multiplicative degree-Kirchhoff index in tree structures, alongside a closed-form solution for unweighted graphs. Numerical illustrations are provided to validate the proposed formulas.

This paper examines the communication requirements for the linear bandit problem within a contextual framework. We introduce a protocol that transmits a compact representation of the context, enabling the receiver to achieve regret scaling with the communication budget $B$ at a rate of $\tilde{O}(d^{3/2}T^{1/2}B^{-1/2})$. This performance matches the theoretical lower bound of $\Omega(T^{1/2}B^{-1/2})$ up to logarithmic factors. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of context distribution on the optimal bit allocation, demonstrating that richer distributions reduce necessary communication bits. Additionally, we present a protocol that transmits a sparse subset of selected contexts, yielding a regret bound of $\tilde{O}(d^{3/2}T^{1/2}B^{-1/2})$, which also aligns with the optimal lower bound of $\Omega(T^{1/2}B^{-1/2})$ up to logarithmic factors.

This study examines the impact of resampling techniques on predictive modeling within class-imbalanced datasets, specifically in the context of the 2016 Kaggle "Credit Card Fraud Detection" competition. By analyzing the relationship between training set size, class distribution, and model performance, the authors demonstrate that the apparent detrimental effects of imbalance are actually neutralized by using an appropriate oversampling strategy. Furthermore, the research highlights that the competition's data exhibited a clear non-linear correlation between transaction amount and fraud status, and that combining this feature with traditional resampling techniques yields optimal results.

We introduce a novel method for analyzing these decays that leverages the interference between $B^0 \to D^{(*)} S \to D K$ processes, where $S$ represents $K^0_{\text{S}}$, $K^+ K^-$, or $D^\pm D^\mp$ mesons. We demonstrate that the interference between $B^0 \to D^{(*)} S \to D K$ processes, where $S$ represents $K^0_{\text{S}}$, $K^+ K^-$, or $D^\pm D^\mp$ mesons, provides a means to measure $a_{\text{S}}$ parameter. A bibliometric analysis of the 2015 Higgs boson discovery demonstrates that bibliographic data can independently validate scientific claims, thereby bolstering the reproducibility of results. By examining citation and co-citation networks, we identify that the papers, experiments, collaborations, and institutions associated with the Higgs announcement form a configuration uniquely associated with high-impact scientific breakthroughs.

The "flying focus X" method, which utilizes a spatial light modulator to create a four-spot cross-shaped focal plane, significantly broadens the application flexibility of pulsed lasers. This configuration offers a versatile platform for investigating various physical phenomena and engineering specific material microstructures. In this study, we present a novel application of this technique to perform simultaneous, dual-site laser machining on silicon wafers. We detail the experimental setup, the resulting morphology, and the underlying physical mechanisms driving the ablation process. Our findings reveal that the cross-shaped beam induces a unique, non-conventional machining pattern. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the cross-beam structure enhances the ablation efficiency of the silicon wafer. These results hold substantial promise for advancing precision manufacturing and microfabrication technologies.

The FIRA HuroCup league, established in 1995, is a prominent platform for advancing humanoid robotics research. In this competition, robots execute tasks inspired by the Olympic Winter Games, specifically freestyle skiing and snowboarding. This paper introduces a novel reinforcement learning framework designed to enhance the performance of these athletes. Our approach utilizes a model-free, off-policy, off-line method that leverages a dataset of expert actions to train agents. This dataset is generated through a specialized exploration algorithm that prioritizes the discovery of high-reward actions. We evaluate this framework against a baseline using the 2019 FIRA HuroCup IV simulation environment. The results demonstrate that our method surpasses the baseline, yielding an average score of 1000 points per run compared to the baseline's 600 points.

Cross-domain recommendation systems (CDRS) are designed to enhance recommendation quality by leveraging data from multiple domains. However, existing approaches often fail to sufficiently exploit the latent semantic relationships between items across different domains. This study introduces a new metric learning framework for CDRS that utilizes a dual objective: maximizing the similarity between items sharing similar user interactions while minimizing the distances between items with divergent user preferences. To achieve this, we develop a specialized metric learning loss function and integrate it with a standard collaborative filtering baseline. Experimental results across three public benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art CDRS techniques.

We examine a model of automaton consisting of finite-state machines (FSM) that communicate through shared variables. We analyze the system's expressive power by varying two key factors: the communication method (shared registers versus non-blocking shared buses) and the presence or absence of synchronization. We demonstrate that this variation significantly impacts the system's capabilities. Specifically, we establish that synchronization is not required for the synchronization-free variant to achieve the expressive power of the full shared-memory Turing machine. Furthermore, we prove that the synchronization-free version with shared buses is strictly more powerful than the same model without buses. Finally, we show that the synchronization-free version is strictly less powerful than the original shared-memory Turing machine.

This study introduces a vibrational model for the heat transfer of 2D complex plasma layers, incorporating vibrational relaxation and the influence of an external transverse electric field. The model is formulated as a system of nonlinear hyperbolic conservation laws, and we investigate the asymptotic behavior of its solutions when vibrational relaxation becomes rapid. By analyzing the system's linearized counterpart, we derive a vibrational relaxation term expansion, which facilitates the construction of both the formal expansion and a rigorous derivation of the corresponding diffusion equation.

This study examines the expressiveness of Coloured Petri nets (CPNs) by utilizing an abstract model known as the ordered $\omega$-counter machine, which serves as a specialized variant of the classical Minsky two-counter machine. The primary objective is to establish a novel, rigorous framework for assessing CPN expressiveness. We demonstrate that this framework is sound and complete by proving a bijective correspondence between the operational semantics of ordered $\omega$-counter machines and the mathematical structures employed to define CPN semantics. Furthermore, we provide a novel proof of the existence of such semantics, which was originally established by Best and Best via a different method. This study introduces a novel approach for synthesizing high frame rate (HFR) coronary angiography (CAG) video from low frame rate (LFR) data. The proposed method employs a deep learning framework that integrates a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) to generate HFR CAG from LFR inputs. The system is trained using a composite loss function combining pixel-level MSE and structural similarity (SSIM) metrics, alongside a temporal consistency loss. The temporal loss specifically penalizes inconsistencies between synthesized frames and their corresponding original frames. Experimental results indicate that the synthesized HFR videos achieve a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 30.9 dB, surpassing the original LFR inputs which had a PSNR of 24.1 dB. Furthermore, the synthesized videos demonstrate strong temporal consistency, with an SSNR of 0.973, compared to 0.951 for the original LFR inputs. Qualitative assessments further confirm that the approach effectively enhances LFR CAG quality while maintaining high temporal coherence.

The FCC-ee project, designed to operate as a $e^+e^-$ collider at center-of-mass energies of 255, 911, and 1625 GeV, is projected to deliver up to $8 \times 10^{36}$ $e^+e^-$ collisions. Operating in an ultra-low-background experimental environment, FCC-ee offers the potential to investigate rare decays of heavy-flavoured particles with exceptional sensitivity. This sensitivity is quantified by the branching fraction ratio $R_{X} = \mathcal{B}(X \to f_1f_2f_3) / \mathcal{B}(X \to cudb)$, where $X$ represents a $B$ or $D$ meson and $f_1f_2f_3$ are any three quarks. This paper outlines the experimental capabilities of FCC-ee in probing these rare decays and reviews the current experimental limits and Standard Model predictions for selected rare $B$ and $D$ meson modes.

Coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering (CE$
u$NS) has been observed in experiments such as COHERENT, DUNE, and ICARUS, and this signal is anticipated to be detectable in future direct dark matter detection facilities. This study examines how the CE$
u$NS discovery influences constraints on the properties of sub-GeV dark matter candidates. We analyze the impact of known neutrino backgrounds on dark matter signals, specifically focusing on the neutrino flux from the Sun and its effect on dark matter parameter limits. Our results indicate that the CE$
u$NS detection tightens the lower bound on the spin-independent dark matter-nucleon cross section by approximately 10% to 20% for masses below 100 MeV, and by roughly 10% to 25% for masses between 100 MeV and 1 GeV.

The gravitational influence of an intermediate-mass companion on the Galactic Center's super-massive black hole (SMBH) can induce orbital precession in stars within the central region. This study examines how such precession affects the orbital characteristics of stars situated within the black hole's sphere of influence. We demonstrate that the dynamics of these stars are significantly altered by the intermediate-mass companion, particularly when the SMBH's orbit around the companion is highly eccentric. In this configuration, the intermediate-mass companion can substantially modify the orbital parameters of stars in the SMBH's sphere of influence.

This study examines stochastic differential equations (SDEs) perturbed by fractional Brownian motion, where the driving noise possesses a Hurst parameter $H$ within the range $(0, 1/2)$. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, varying the Hurst parameter toward $H + \delta$ ($\delta > 0$) induces a non-trivial modification to the law of the solution. This finding offers a novel approach for quantifying sensitivity to the Hurst parameter.

We demonstrate that the nonstationary ideal on $\omega_1$ is Σ¹ definable with a set-parameter whenever either of these scenarios holds: the existence of a Suslin tree, or the equivalence of the nonstationary and stationary ideals on the cardinality of the continuum.

Multitask training has recently gained significant attention, offering a method to enhance performance across various tasks by leveraging shared representations. However, the field currently lacks a standardized benchmark for evaluating these approaches. To address this, we introduce a systematic experimental framework designed to facilitate multitask training research. We demonstrate the framework's utility through experiments on a task set comprising machine translation, text classification, and sequence labeling. Our findings indicate that the proposed methodology can uncover new strategies for improving multitask performance.

Traffic sign recognition is a critical area of research within computer vision, with the development of large-scale datasets playing a pivotal role in advancing transfer learning and enhancing detection performance. This study introduces Traffic Sign Dataset (TSDS), a comprehensive collection comprising 100,000 images across 10 distinct categories. The dataset is designed to facilitate the training of robust deep learning models for traffic sign detection. Experimental results demonstrate that pre-training on TSDS significantly boosts the performance of detection algorithms. Furthermore, the dataset is publicly accessible at http://www.zhaozhao.net/TSDS.

In recent years, recommender systems have become ubiquitous, yet their performance is often hindered by the scarcity of labeled data. While recent studies have explored using self-supervised learning (SCL) to address this issue, these methods typically rely on pre-training a model before fine-tuning it on downstream tasks, a process that is both computationally expensive and slow. To overcome these limitations, we introduce SelfCF, a new framework designed to achieve rapid and accurate training. SelfCF integrates a self-supervised pre-training phase with a recommendation task under a unified model, eliminating the need for separate pre-training and fine-tuning steps. This approach not only accelerates the training process but also outperforms conventional supervised methods in recommendation accuracy. We conducted extensive experiments on four standard benchmarks, comparing SelfCF against state-of-the-art baselines. The results demonstrate that SelfCF attains superior recommendation accuracy while reducing training time by 40% and inference time by 50%.

This study investigates the count of unramified and partially ramified coverings defined over a curve of genus $g$. We demonstrate that augmenting classical Riemann-Hurwitz constraints with specific extra ramification requirements allows these counting problems to be resolved through the mechanism of logarithmic degeneration combined with an induction argument applied to the curve's genus.

This study examines the high-energy density of states and optical conductivity within a gapped Dirac semimetal, utilizing the gapped Dirac equation to model the optical conductivity. We find that the density of states follows a linear dependence on energy at high energies, consistent with the behavior of a gapless Dirac semimetal; however, the gap significantly alters the optical conductivity spectrum. Specifically, the optical conductivity exhibits a pronounced peak at finite frequencies, a feature that diminishes as the gap size decreases.

This study examines a slow-fast differential equation model representing a predator-prey scenario with periodic coefficients, where the frequency varies inversely with a large parameter. We analyze how the system's behavior changes as this large parameter increases, focusing on the emergence of multiple limit cycles. Our findings reveal that slow-fast dynamics with periodic coefficients exhibit distinct properties compared to non-periodic counterparts. Specifically, we demonstrate that the system can generate multiple limit cycles, a phenomenon not observed in systems with non-periodic forcing.

Third-generation gravitational wave observatories are anticipated to detect numerous binary black hole mergers with exceptional sensitivity. This study investigates the observability of higher-order modes (HOs) in such systems, specifically focusing on the (3,3) and (4,4) modes. Utilizing a population of 1000 binary black hole mergers from the GWTC-3 catalog, we simulated these events using the IMRPhenomPv2 waveform model. Our analysis reveals that (3,3) and (4,4) modes are detectable in 90% and 70% of these mergers, respectively, for both third-generation detectors, GW A and Einstein Telescope. Furthermore, the study indicates that these modes are more readily observed in systems with higher mass ratios and higher inclination angles.

The Gaia mission is expected to detect a vast array of astrometric binaries, among which are those involving black holes (BHs). This study examines the orbital characteristics of such systems, specifically analyzing the relationship between orbital radius and the velocity of the visible component. This relationship is defined by a radius of curvature, which is derived from the arc traced by the star on the sky plane. We demonstrate that for systems with a black hole companion, this velocity versus radius relationship exhibits a distinct non-linear feature. This signature is a robust indicator of a dark companion, as it is independent of the black hole's mass and unaffected by the viewing angle. Furthermore, we show that this signature is a universal signature of astrometric binaries with massive companions, applicable to any star-black hole pair, as well as star-neutron star or star-Wolf-Rayet systems. This study examines how crossover and selection mechanisms influence the performance of genetic algorithms (GAs) in solving the 0/1 knapsack problem. We evaluated four crossover operators—uniform, arithmetic, geometric, and simulated binary—paired with two selection methods—roulette wheel and tournament. Experiments were conducted on four datasets comprising 10, 50, 100, and 500 items. The results indicate that the simulated binary crossover operator combined with the roulette wheel selection strategy achieves the highest convergence rate.

Instead, these oscillatory functions are defined via a general mapping $\Phi: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$. The analysis relies on a partitioning method that divides the domain $\mathbb{R}^n$ into regions where the oscillation magnitude is either small or large. In the small oscillation case, we apply the method of stationary phase, whereas the large oscillation case is handled by reducing the problem to a simpler oscillatory integral. We introduce a novel approach to lower the computational expense of Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) calculations for materials featuring high valence electron counts. This method leverages the QMC-to-DFT ratio, computed using low-cost configurations, to adjust Density Functional Theory energies and forces into accurate QMC equivalents. Our findings indicate that the computational cost of determining QMC energies and forces scales with approximately the 2.5th power of the effective pseudopotential valence charge. Consequently, our technique offers a significant reduction in the burden of QMC simulations for systems with high valence electron counts.

This study examines the spread of false claims regarding voter fraud on Twitter during the 2020 U.S. elections, analyzing how these narratives influenced public discourse and how the platform addressed them. By examining a sample of 1.5 million tweets, we identified a surge in misinformation, particularly around the term "fasc fraud," which saw a 1,000% spike in mentions within the first 10 days of election day. Our analysis reveals that these tweets were predominantly retweeted by users with low follower counts, suggesting that while platforms like Twitter played a significant role in amplifying these narratives, the primary audience consists of content creators rather than mass adopters. Furthermore, we found that Twitter's moderation actions were inconsistent, with official responses often lagging behind the initial viral spread of false information. Ultimately, our research underscores the platform's dual-edged role: serving as both a critical vector for the rapid dissemination of disinformation and an imperfect but necessary mechanism for eventual correction.

We demonstrate that for a generic $C^1$ Anosov diffeomorphism $f$ on a compact Riemannian manifold $M$, there exists a set $E$ of points exhibiting high emergence, with $\dim_H(E) > 0$. Specifically, for any $C^1$ SRB measure $\mu$ associated with $f$, every point in $M$ belongs to this set $E$. Moreover, we prove that for a residual set of $C^1$ diffeomorphisms possessing an SRB measure, the Hausdorff dimension of this set $E$ equals the dimension of the entire manifold $M$.

Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are widely utilized for dimensionality reduction, a technique that can enhance the efficiency of deep Bayesian neural networks (DBNNNs) by decreasing the number of input features. This study investigates the application of VAEs to improve feature extraction within DBNNNNs, specifically analyzing how the VAE's architecture and the resulting feature distributions affect the posterior distributions of the subsequent neural network. We demonstrate that VAEs can effectively reduce feature counts while maintaining high classification accuracy. Furthermore, we examine the impact of VAEs on uncertainty quantification, a key advantage of Bayesian networks. Our findings indicate that VAEs can improve uncertainty estimates in specific scenarios, though they may also lead to overconfident predictions in others.

This study introduces a new instanton-based methodology for investigating electron transfer reactions, specifically targeting cases where the Marcus theory framework is insufficient. By integrating the instanton formalism with the classical Marcus theory, we developed a streamlined approach to determine the instanton action. This integration enables the evaluation of tunneling probabilities across the entire potential energy surface, facilitating a comprehensive analysis of reaction mechanisms. We applied this technique to investigate the proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) reaction in the reduction of 2,3-dichloro-1,4-benzoquinone (2,3-DCQ) by the ferrocenium/ferrocene redox couple. Our findings indicate that the instanton theory successfully captures the reaction mechanism, revealing that tunneling is the primary driver of the reaction. Furthermore, the tunneling pathway exhibits a distinct "saddle point" structure, characterized by a specific proton transfer coordinate that varies with the reaction's electronic state.

This study introduces a new framework for enhancing trajectory tracking in robotic systems, accounting for unmodeled dynamics. The methodology integrates a neural network-based disturbance observer with a model-based controller, utilizing a specific algorithm to estimate the influence of these unmodeled dynamics on tracking errors. This algorithm leverages the relationship between such dynamics and the error across various states and time steps. The controller is then designed using a model reference system, with a feedback gain selected to ensure stability and performance. The approach is validated through simulations of a two-link robotic manipulator, demonstrating its effectiveness.

This study examines the electronic, thermoelectric, and magnetotransport characteristics of the $\text{La}_{0.8}\text{Sr}_{0.2}\text{Ca}_{0.1}\text{TiO}_3$ alloy, which contains a tungsten-derived impurity band. The impurity band, situated between the valence and conduction bands, significantly alters the material's electrical conductivity and thermoelectric power. Furthermore, the magnetotransport behavior is governed by the interplay between the two bands, which is further modulated by the impurity band's density of states.

This study introduces a probabilistic framework for the perfect sum problem, wherein a set of $n$ positive integers is provided, and the goal is to determine if their subset sums to a specific target $S$. By leveraging established number-theoretic principles, the approach estimates the likelihood of achieving the target sum. This estimation yields a solution that is both highly accurate and rapid, operating in $O(n \log n)$ time complexity. Furthermore, we examine the application of this method to the analysis of the riemann zeta function.

The method relies on two key observations: first, if a polynomial $x^n - a$ is irreducible over a field $K$, then an element $\alpha$ satisfying $\alpha^n = a + \delta$ (for some $\delta \in K$) is primitive provided $\alpha^n \neq 1$. Second, this approach leverages the fact that irreducibility can be verified in $O(M_n)$ time using the Berlekamp-Rabin test. This paper examines the evolution of strategy synthesis methods for parallel software, tracing their roots to model checking. It details recent technological advances in model checking that have fueled the development of strategy synthesis algorithms for parallel systems. Furthermore, it introduces the concept of model-based strategy synthesis and explores the application of these methods in the domain of autonomous vehicles.

This study introduces a novel, optimized metasurface imaging system designed to mitigate noise and enhance performance. By utilizing a single metasurface capable of simultaneously focusing light and encoding information, we achieve a significant reduction in potential error sources. Furthermore, our approach leverages a machine learning-driven design methodology to create a custom surface that integrates information encoding into the focusing process. This strategy maximizes the signal-to-noise ratio, thereby boosting system efficacy. We validate the feasibility of this concept through both theoretical analysis and experimental demonstrations.

This study investigates the dynamics of high harmonic generation (HHG) in hydrogen under the influence of a linearly polarized laser field, utilizing the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. The analysis focuses on how varying pulse durations and field strengths affect the creation of Rydberg states, as well as the resulting spectral characteristics. The findings indicate that a laser pulse with a field strength of 0.05 a.u. and a duration of 120 fs generates a continuum spectrum, whereas extending the pulse duration to 150 fs produces a spectrum featuring distinct Rydberg states. Additionally, at a field strength of 1.0 a.u. and a pulse duration of 120 fs, the resulting spectrum exhibits a prominent plateau.

Semi-supervised learning (SSL) has garnered significant attention due to its ability to leverage vast amounts of unlabeled data. While recent advancements have shown that SSL can substantially enhance the performance of pre-trained models, these methods often fail to fully utilize the rich information present in unlabeled inputs. This paper introduces a novel SSL framework that utilizes a pre-trained model to generate augmented versions of the unlabeled data by extracting features from multiple source images. By synthesizing these multi-image features, the approach constructs a more comprehensive augmented sample that better represents the underlying semantic content. This method is subsequently applied to existing SSL architectures, yielding marked improvements in their effectiveness. Experimental results on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets demonstrate that this technique achieves state-of-the-art performance across various SSL benchmarks.

This study introduces a new framework for designing experiments to estimate parameters in stochastic gene expression models. We model mRNA copy numbers as a continuous-time Markov chain, where transcription and translation occur as independent Poisson processes driven by time-varying rates. These rates are governed by a polynomial function of protein concentration, representing negative feedback loops. By integrating the master equation with an approximation of the protein distribution, we derive a system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) that describe the mean dynamics. The primary objective is to identify the model parameters that best fit observed data from single-cell experiments. To achieve this, we employ an iterative design strategy that selects experimental conditions maximizing the information gained about the parameters. We demonstrate that our approach yields superior designs compared to those generated by a naive method, and we illustrate its practical utility through applications to synthetic gene circuits.

This study introduces a novel framework for acquiring optimal graph hyperparameters within machine learning contexts. We demonstrate that the efficacy of graph-based algorithms is frequently contingent upon the alignment between their hyperparameters and the intrinsic characteristics of the data. By decoupling hyperparameter optimization from data distribution selection, our approach enables algorithms to adapt to varying data scenarios. We validate this method using graph convolutional networks (GCNs) for node classification, showing that jointly optimizing both hyperparameters and data distribution selection yields superior performance compared to optimizing hyperparameters alone. Additionally, we present a new algorithm for approximating these learned distributions and conduct an empirical analysis of the resulting model's generalization capabilities.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a promising near-term variational approach for addressing combinatorial optimization tasks. This study examines the impact of coherent dephasing errors on QAOA training dynamics, specifically within the context of the Max-Cut problem. Our analysis reveals that these errors can induce premature convergence to suboptimal local minima. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the detrimental influence of such errors can be mitigated by incorporating an additional layer (p-level) into the QAOA circuit.

Person Re-Identification (ReID) has attracted considerable attention within the computer vision community due to its practical utility in security and surveillance. However, the task remains highly challenging because of the inherent diversity in appearance and the scarcity of training data. While existing methods have primarily focused on extracting discriminative features from images, they have largely overlooked the valuable information contained in image captions. This paper introduces a novel framework that leverages natural language descriptions to enhance ReID performance. Our approach utilizes a multi-modal feature learning strategy, where image and text features are jointly learned to create a unified embedding space. By employing a contrastive loss function, we ensure that features from matching images and their corresponding captions are positioned closer together in this shared space. Furthermore, we incorporate a triplet loss function to optimize the inter-class separation between different individuals. Experimental results on standard benchmarks demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art solutions.

This study introduces a novel approach for generating high-fidelity time series data of power system states and control variables. The method utilizes the actual physics of the system alongside actual measurements to synthesize a dataset of high-quality trajectories. The process involves two main steps: first, a data-driven model of the system dynamics is constructed by analyzing recorded data; second, a trajectory is generated by simulating the system using this learned model. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through a case study of a real-world 138 kV substation.

This study examines the convergence behavior of perturbed iterative algorithms applied to variational inequality problems within nonexpansive mappings defined on Hilbert spaces. Specifically, we establish that these processes converge to a unique solution under certain conditions. Furthermore, we derive an estimate for the convergence rate. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted to validate the theoretical findings.
